sub_answers.sub_question: What degeneracies exist between eccentricity, mass ratio, spin, and distance in gravitational-wave parameter estimation?
What astrophysical formation channels predict high-eccentricity black hole mergers and how uncertain are their event-rate predictions?
sub_answers.text: Hierarchical triples, such as those in globular clusters and galactic nuclei, are predicted to produce observable large eccentricity at LIGO frequencies [d42403s0p0]. Three-body interactions in globular clusters are estimated to produce significant eccentricity for roughly 5% of mergers entering the 10 Hz band [d44584s0p0]. Repeated/second-generation mergers in hierarchical systems like 2+2 quadruples can produce eccentric and mass-gap events, but second-generation mergers are estimated to be about 10^7 times less common than first-generation mergers [d65715s0p0]. Scattering and secular dynamical interactions in hierarchical systems can produce a small subset of highly eccentric LIGO sources, indicating event-rate predictions for these channels are strongly suppressed compared to isolated binaries and thus uncertain [d65715s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are the dominant sources of systematic error (waveform model inaccuracies, detector calibration, selection effects) affecting H0 from GW events like GW190521?
How do limited sky localization and lack of electromagnetic counterparts constrain host identification and redshift determination for GW190521?
How would revising GW190521's inferred luminosity distance under an eccentric-merger model change its contribution to a gravitational-wave H0 posterior?
What statistical methods combine single-event distance measurements from gravitational waves into joint H0 estimates, and how sensitive are they to outlier events?
How can eccentric-merger interpretations affect the use of galaxy catalogs or redshift priors when associating GW190521 with host galaxies?
What practical changes in data analysis pipelines are required to incorporate eccentric waveform models into standard siren H0 inference?
What were the reported primary observational properties (masses, spins, sky localization, luminosity distance) of GW190521?
What observational signatures distinguish an eccentric binary black hole merger from a circular one in gravitational-wave data?
sub_answers.text: Eccentric binaries exhibit an oscillatory frequency evolution that can cause gravitational-wave frequencies to recur multiple times through coalescence [d110908s0p0]. Eccentric signals can have different durations and signal-to-noise ratios compared to quasi-circular mergers, with eccentric mergers sometimes producing larger SNRs for second-generation detectors and shorter time-span signals than circular ones of the same mass [d60694s0p0]. Eccentric systems can excite additional waveform structure and subdominant modes that affect sky localization and waveform morphology compared to purely (2,2)-mode circular signals [d110908s0p0]. Eccentric binaries tend to circularize in the last few cycles before merger, so residual eccentricity appears primarily in the inspiral and causes measurable phase differences relative to circular post-Newtonian models [d39658s0p0][d2843s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What is the physical definition of the Hubble constant (H0) and how is it estimated using gravitational-wave standard sirens?
What are typical detection sensitivities and selection biases of LIGO/Virgo for high-mass, short-duration signals like GW190521?
How does nonzero orbital eccentricity modify the gravitational-wave waveform morphology compared to quasi-circular templates?
sub_answers.text: Eccentric binaries show oscillatory, recurrent frequency evolution with multiple passages of the same GW frequencies rather than the monotonic chirp of quasi-circular signals [d110908s0p0]. [d94650s0p0] Eccentricity produces amplitude, phase, and frequency modulations that are common across spherical-harmonic modes and can be modeled as a single time-series modulation on otherwise quasi-circular waveforms [d94650s0p0]. Periastron passages excite neutron-star f-modes which transfer orbital energy to stellar oscillations and advance the GW phase relative to circular cases, producing larger cumulative phase shifts for higher eccentricities [d51623s0p0]. Inclusion of subdominant (higher-order) modes becomes more important with eccentricity, increasing SNR and altering morphology compared to pure (2,2)-mode quasi-circular templates [d79698s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are the effects of eccentricity on measured source-frame versus detector-frame masses and inferred redshift?
How does eccentricity-induced waveform complexity affect Bayesian parameter estimation and distance uncertainty for compact binaries?
sub_answers.text: Neglecting eccentricity can create degeneracies with other low-frequency effects (e.g., line-of-sight acceleration), biasing parameter recovery unless both effects are modeled and thereby impacting Bayesian inference [d131516s0p0]. Including eccentricity and subdominant modes improves detection SNR and sky localization, reducing sky-area uncertainties substantially and providing extra early-warning time compared to circular templates [d110908s0p0]. Injection studies show that when both eccentricity and external-acceleration effects are included in templates the true parameters are recovered within 90% credible intervals, demonstrating that modeling eccentricity reduces bias in posterior estimates [d131516s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What waveform models and approximations exist for eccentric binary black holes and how do their systematic errors compare?
sub_answers.text: Available eccentric BBH waveform tools include numerical-relativity catalogs (SXS, RIT), effective-one-body models like TEOBResumS-Dali and SEOBNRE, and phenomenological conversions such as gwNRHME that map quasi-circular quadrupolar waveforms to multi-modal eccentric waveforms [d101479s0p0][d79698s0p0][d94650s0p0]. Systematic errors vary by model and mode content: inclusion of higher-order modes increases recovered SNR by a few to tens of percent for eccentric signals, and the gwNRHME model achieves mismatches ~10^{-3} against NR simulations, comparable to NR numerical errors [d79698s0p0][d94650s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: For gravitational-wave parameter estimation, what are the quantitative degeneracies (e.g., posterior covariances, Fisher-matrix correlations) among orbital eccentricity, component mass ratio, individual spins (magnitudes and tilt angles), and luminosity distance? Provide which parameter pairs show the strongest correlations for short, intermediate, and long-duration signals, how those correlations change with SNR and waveform family (time-domain vs frequency-domain, precessing vs non-precessing), and concrete examples from real events (e.g., GW190521) and synthetic injections showing typical bias sizes when degeneracies are ignored.

Which astrophysical formation pathways specifically predict substantial residual orbital eccentricity at LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA band frequencies (e.g., ≥0.1 at 10 Hz or eccentricity ~0.7 at 0.1 Hz): dynamical interactions in dense star clusters (globular, nuclear star clusters), hierarchical mergers in clusters, Lidov–Kozai oscillations in triple systems, migration and capture in active galactic nucleus (AGN) disks, and primordial black-hole scenarios? For each channel give predicted eccentricity distributions as a function of GW frequency, the central predicted volumetric merger rates with uncertainty ranges (min/median/max), and the key modeling assumptions that drive those rate uncertainties.

What are the primary sources of systematic error that bias a gravitational-wave-based Hubble constant measurement from a single high-mass event like GW190521: waveform-model systematics (missing eccentricity, precession, higher multipoles), detector calibration amplitude/phase uncertainties, selection effects and population priors, gravitational lensing magnification, and peculiar velocities of candidate host galaxies? For each source quantify expected bias or additional uncertainty on distance/H0 (e.g., percent-level or absolute km/s/Mpc) and summarize how different analysis choices (waveform families, calibration marginalization, selection-function modeling) change the result.

Given GW190521-like data, how do the size and morphology of the GW sky localization region, the completeness and depth of galaxy catalogs at probable redshifts (z ~ 0.5–1.5), and the absence of an electromagnetic counterpart limit confident host-galaxy identification and redshift assignment? Include: typical credible-region areas and multimodality for such short, loud signals; galaxy-counting and ranking methods (weighted by luminosity/mass/star-formation); the effect of catalog incompleteness and spectroscopic vs photometric redshift errors on host probability; and how these factors propagate into redshift uncertainty and H0 posterior width for GW190521-like events.

If GW190521's luminosity distance posterior were recalculated using eccentric-binary waveform models (e.g., SEOBNRE, TEOBResumS with eccentric corrections), how would that modified distance posterior numerically alter the event's weight in a combined gravitational-wave measurement of H0 compared to the circular-binary assumption?

Which combination techniques (hierarchical Bayesian modeling, inverse-variance weighted likelihood stacking, Bayesian model averaging, or bootstrap/meta-analysis) are used to merge per-event gravitational-wave distance posteriors into a joint H0 posterior, and how do each of these approaches respond quantitatively to a single discrepant event (outlier) with a shifted distance distribution?

In what ways would interpreting GW190521 as an eccentric merger change the probabilistic association between the event and catalogued galaxies (e.g., GLADE, DES, SDSS) — specifically, how would eccentricity-modified distance and sky-localization posteriors alter the computed host-galaxy posterior probabilities and the resulting redshift prior used for H0 inference?

What concrete modifications are needed in an end-to-end standard-siren H0 pipeline to include eccentric waveforms: which waveform families and parameter priors must be added, what sampling and likelihood-evaluation changes are required, and how do these affect computational cost, convergence diagnostics, and marginalization over selection effects?

Give the reported parameter-estimation results for GW190521: median and 90% credible intervals (or credible regions) for primary and secondary source-frame and detector-frame masses, effective aligned and precession spin parameters (e.g., χeff, χp), inferred mass ratio, sky localization area and credible sky map coordinates, and luminosity distance with uncertainties; note differences between waveform models or analysis choices if reported.

List the measurable gravitational-wave features that indicate nonzero orbital eccentricity at merger versus a quasi-circular binary: specific differences in the time–frequency track (e.g., multiple periastron bursts, faster frequency sweeps), presence and relative power of higher harmonics and noninteger mode structure, phase evolution departures from post-Newtonian circular templates, transient amplitude/phase modulations, and how these affect matched-filter residuals and parameter-estimation posteriors.
sub_answers.text: Eccentric binaries show an oscillatory frequency evolution with GW frequencies that can recur multiple times through coalescence (multiple periastron passages) rather than a single monotonic chirp [d110908s0p0]. Eccentricity produces stronger relative power in subdominant harmonics and higher-order modes compared to quasicircular binaries, improving the contribution of those modes to localization and signal power [d110908s0p0]. Orbital eccentricity induces phase-evolution departures from circular post-Newtonian templates which appear as specific phase corrections to the leading (2,2) harmonic and can mimic other low-frequency effects if not modelled [d131516s0p0]. Eccentricity can cause transient amplitude and phase modulations (periastron bursts) that change the time–frequency track and can leave excess matched-filter residuals or broaden posteriors when circular templates are used [d110908s0p0][d131516s0p0]. Neglecting eccentricity in templates can bias or degenerate inferred parameters (e.g., recovering LOSA or other low-frequency effects instead of true eccentricity), thereby affecting matched-filter residuals and parameter-estimation posteriors [d131516s0p0][d121579s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Give a concise physical definition of the Hubble constant (H0) (the proportionality between recession velocity and distance in the local Universe) and then explain, step-by-step, how gravitational-wave ‘standard sirens’ measure H0: how the GW signal yields a luminosity distance, how redshift is obtained or marginalized over (bright siren host galaxy redshift, dark-siren statistical galaxy-catalog method, or EM counterpart), the basic measurement equation linking redshift, distance and H0, and the main sources of statistical and systematic uncertainty in the GW-based H0 estimate.
sub_answers.text: The Hubble constant H0 is the proportionality between recessional velocity and distance in the local Universe (i.e., the expansion rate today) [d61893s0p0]. Gravitational-wave standard sirens measure H0 because the GW amplitude and phasing encode the source luminosity distance directly from the waveform, providing a distance measurement independent of the cosmic distance ladder [d61893s0p0]. Redshift is obtained either from an electromagnetic counterpart/host-galaxy redshift for a "bright" siren, or statistically/marginally from galaxy catalogs or population assumptions for "dark" sirens; these redshifts are then paired with the GW distance to infer H0 (as exemplified by using a candidate EM counterpart ZTF19abanrhr at z=0.438 for GW190521) [d61893s0p0]. The basic measurement links observed luminosity distance dL from the GW to redshift z through the cosmological distance–redshift relation (which depends on H0 and other cosmological parameters) and estimates H0 by fitting that relation to the measured dL–z pairs [d61893s0p0]. Main sources of statistical and systematic uncertainty include GW distance uncertainty and waveform/modeling choices, noise and PSD estimation, spin priors and analysis choices, and unmodeled physical effects (e.g., eccentricity or line-of-sight acceleration) that can bias distance or other parameter estimates [d61893s0p0][d57075s0p0][d131516s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Describe typical LIGO/Virgo detection sensitivity and selection effects relevant to high-total-mass, short-duration signals like GW190521: frequency band and network SNR thresholds, fitted-match-filter efficiency as a function of total mass and mass ratio, horizon distances for such heavy systems, reduced number of inspiral cycles and its impact on parameter recovery (especially mass, spin, and sky localization), biases toward detecting face-on/face-off orientations and aligned spins, and known pipeline limitations or completeness issues for very short, high-mass transients.

In what specific ways do nonzero orbital eccentricities alter the time- and frequency-domain gravitational-wave signal (harmonic content, phasing evolution, merger-ringdown timing) relative to waveforms from binaries on quasi-circular orbits?
sub_answers.text: Eccentric binaries produce additional harmonic content compared to quasi-circular signals, with leading eccentric harmonics (e.g., (2,2) plus multiple sideband harmonics) appearing in the waveform [d50914s0p0]. Eccentricity alters the phasing evolution, producing cumulative phase shifts and periastron-advance corrections that must be included in the GW phase to high PN order for accurate modelling [d50914s0p0]. Periastron passages and tidal excitations in eccentric neutron-star binaries can accelerate orbital decay and advance the GW phase, producing phase jumps and earlier merger timing relative to circular inspirals [d51623s0p0]. Many eccentric BBH systems circularize in the last few cycles before merger, allowing the use of quasi-circular merger and ringdown pieces in hybrid models, though residual eccentric effects persist up to the final cycles for modest eccentricities (e_ref ≲ 0.08) and can affect the precise merger-ringdown timing [d39658s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does orbital eccentricity bias or modify the mapping between observed (detector-frame) masses and inferred source-frame masses and cosmological redshift, and what magnitude of mass/redshift error arises for typical stellar-mass and intermediate-mass binaries at different eccentricities?

How does the additional structure introduced by eccentric orbits (multiple harmonics, periastron precession, rapid phase jumps) impact Bayesian parameter-estimation posteriors — in particular sky localization, luminosity distance and mass–spin degeneracies — and how does recovered distance uncertainty scale with eccentricity and SNR?

Which families of eccentric waveform approximants (e.g., PN-based eccentric Taylor models, EOB with eccentric extensions, numerical-relativity hybrids, frequency-domain kludge models) are available for eccentric binary black holes, what parameter ranges do they cover, and what are the dominant sources and magnitudes of systematic error when these models are used for parameter inference?
sub_answers.text: PN-based frequency-domain inspiral templates that include eccentric amplitude corrections and high-PN-order eccentric phase evolution (up to 3PN with eccentricity expanded to sixth order per PN order) are available for moderately eccentric inspirals [d50914s0p0]. Effective-one-body (EOB) waveform models with eccentric or dynamical-capture extensions exist that cover arbitrary mass ratios and nonprecessing spins and can model direct plunges and successive close encounters relevant for highly eccentric/dynamical-capture events [d61816s0p0]. Numerical-relativity calibrated eccentric inspiral–merger–ringdown hybrid models exist for nonspinning BBHs with e_ref ≲ 0.08 and mass ratios q ≤ 3 and are tuned to NR waveforms starting ~20 cycles before merger, achieving high faithfulness for sufficiently massive systems [d39658s0p0]. Dominant sources of systematic error reported are limited eccentricity calibration range and use of quasi-circular merger pieces (residual eccentric effects when e_ref ≳ 0.05), truncation of PN orders and eccentric expansions, and limited NR coverage for high eccentricity or large mass-ratio encounters; these limitations lead to mismatches at the percent level, with reported faithfulness ≥97% for M ≥ 85 M_⊙ (e_ref ≤ 0.08) and slightly stricter eccentric limits for lower total masses [d39658s0p0][d50914s0p0][d61816s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How do correlations between orbital eccentricity, component mass ratio, black-hole spins (magnitudes and orientations), and luminosity distance bias posterior distributions in gravitational-wave parameter estimation pipelines (e.g., bilby, LALInference), and which summary statistics show the strongest degeneracies?

Which astrophysical channels (dynamical encounters in globular clusters and nuclear star clusters, Kozai-Lidov in triples, gas-assisted migration in AGN disks, primordial black-hole scenarios) are predicted to produce highly eccentric (e > 0.1 at LIGO band) binary black-hole mergers, and what are the current uncertainties and model-dependent ranges for their predicted volumetric merger rates?

For events like GW190521, what are the leading systematic error contributions to inferred H0 arising from imperfect waveform models (neglect of eccentricity or higher modes), detector calibration uncertainties, and selection biases (detection pipeline selection functions and population priors), and what are typical magnitudes of those errors reported in the literature?

Given GW190521's broad sky map and absence of an electromagnetic counterpart, how do sky-localization area, distance uncertainty, galaxy catalog incompleteness, and probability-weighted host ranking algorithms limit secure host-galaxy identification and spectroscopic redshift assignment, and what redshift uncertainty does that imply for cosmological use?

If GW190521 were reanalyzed with an eccentric-merger waveform yielding a different posterior on luminosity distance, how would that change the event's likelihood contribution and weight in a combined gravitational-wave measurement of H0 (e.g., via reweighted single-event posteriors or updated distance-redshift kernels)?
sub_answers.text: A reanalysis that produces a different luminosity-distance posterior will change GW190521's likelihood contribution because the event's per-event distance posterior directly enters joint H0 inference and alters the event weight in reweighted single-event posterior combinations [d61893s0p0]. Different waveform models already produced substantially different H0 medians and credible intervals for GW190521, demonstrating that a shifted distance posterior can materially move the combined H0 posterior when that event is included [d61893s0p0]. Updated eccentric waveform posteriors would therefore change the distance–redshift kernel used for that event and so change its influence in hierarchical or importance-sampling combinations of events [d101479s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which specific statistical combination techniques (hierarchical Bayesian models, importance-sampling of single-event posteriors, inverse-variance weighting, bootstrap or robust-estimator approaches) are used to merge individual GW distance measurements into a joint H0 posterior, and what analyses (influence functions, leave-one-out tests, or simulation studies) quantify their sensitivity to an outlier event like GW190521?

In what ways could interpreting GW190521 as an eccentric merger change how galaxy catalogs or redshift priors are used for host association — for example by altering the distance PDF overlap with candidate galaxies, shifting galaxy ranking metrics, modifying completeness corrections, or changing the posterior probability for specific catalog entries?

What concrete modifications to standard-siren H0 analysis pipelines are needed to adopt eccentric waveform models — e.g., adding eccentric templates to parameter-estimation codes, updating prior ranges and sampling strategies, recalculating selection functions via injection campaigns with eccentric signals, and accounting for increased computational cost or waveform systematics in the H0 hierarchical inference?
sub_answers.text: Pipelines would need to include eccentric waveform models in parameter-estimation codes so posteriors reflect eccentric dynamics rather than circular approximations [d94650s0p0]. Prior ranges and sampling strategies should be extended to cover eccentricity and any correlated parameters to avoid biases and degeneracies (e.g., with line-of-sight acceleration or low-frequency phase effects) [d131516s0p0]. Selection functions and detection efficiencies must be recalculated with injection campaigns that use eccentric signals to obtain correct population weights and search sensitivities [d101479s0p0]. Analysis frameworks must account for waveform-model systematics and potentially higher computational cost from larger template banks or more expensive eccentric waveforms, and modular waveform additions (such as the gwNRHME modulation) can reduce modelling complexity and aid integration [d94650s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: List the published parameter-estimation results for GW190521 from major analyses (LIGO/Virgo collaboration and independent groups): source-frame and detector-frame component masses with credible intervals, final remnant mass and radiated energy, individual and effective spins (chi_eff, chi_p) with uncertainties, sky localization credible region (area at 90% and 50%), luminosity distance and redshift posteriors, network signal-to-noise ratio and which waveform models produced these estimates.

Which concrete, measurable waveform features indicate nonzero orbital eccentricity in a BBH merger: e.g., deviations in the inspiral phase evolution compared with circular templates, presence of higher-frequency periastron-like bursts, persistent harmonic content or frequency modulation in time–frequency spectrograms, mismatches and residuals when fitting circular templates, constraints on eccentricity parameter e at a reference frequency (e.g. 10 Hz) from parameter estimation, and how these signatures can be confused with or distinguished from effects of precession or higher-order modes?
sub_answers.text: Nonzero orbital eccentricity produces deviations in the inspiral-phase evolution relative to circular templates that can be measured as phase corrections in the (2,2) mode and leading eccentric harmonics [d101479s0p0][d131516s0p0]. Eccentric binaries show oscillatory frequency evolution and recurrent passages of higher instantaneous frequency near periastron, which can appear as higher-frequency or burst-like features in the time–frequency track compared with a smooth chirp [d110908s0p0][d60694s0p0]. Persistent additional harmonic content and frequency modulation (multiple harmonics and non-monotonic frequency evolution) are signatures of eccentricity visible in spectrograms and in waveform harmonic structure [d101479s0p0][d110908s0p0]. Significant mismatches and coherent residuals when fitting circular templates indicate eccentricity if eccentric waveform templates reduce those mismatches, and parameter-estimation constraints are often reported as upper limits or posteriors on eccentricity at a reference frequency (e.g., e at 10 Hz or similar) [d101479s0p0][d121579s0p0]. Eccentricity signatures can be confused or partially degenerate with other low-frequency effects such as line-of-sight acceleration, and with precession or higher-order modes, so joint modeling (including LOSA, precession and higher modes) is required to distinguish them robustly [d131516s0p0][d110908s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Provide a concise physical definition of the Hubble constant H0 (units and its role in cosmology, e.g. v ≈ H0 d at low redshift and H0 as H(t0) from the Friedmann equation), and describe step-by-step how gravitational-wave ‘standard sirens’ measure H0: how the GW amplitude gives an absolute luminosity distance (including dependence on inclination and calibration), how a redshift is obtained either from an electromagnetic counterpart or statistical galaxy–host association, the basic formula used to infer H0 and the dominant sources of uncertainty (distance error, redshift/host ambiguity, peculiar velocities, weak lensing, calibration), plus examples of single-event vs population (dark siren) approaches.

What are the typical LIGO/Virgo detection sensitivities and selection effects specifically for very high total-mass, short-duration BBH signals like GW190521: include typical amplitude spectral density and sensitive frequency band relevant for 50–500+ M⊙ mergers, approximate horizon / sensitive distance scaling as a function of total mass, network SNR thresholds and detection efficiency for short signals, how duration and high mass reduce matched-filter sensitivity and sky-localization precision (typical 90% credible areas), template-bank and search-pipeline inefficiencies for eccentric or highly spinning short signals, and quantitative examples of selection bias (preferential detection of face-on, higher-mass, higher-SNR orientations) and how these biases affect population inferences.

In what specific ways does a nonzero orbital eccentricity alter the observed gravitational-wave waveform shape relative to quasi-circular templates — e.g., additional harmonic content, periastron “bursts,” modified instantaneous frequency evolution and phase modulation — and how do these changes depend on eccentricity magnitude, orbital phase at observation, and mass ratio?
sub_answers.text: Eccentricity introduces additional harmonic content in the waveform beyond the dominant (2,2) mode, producing multiple eccentric harmonics in the Fourier-domain response [d50914s0p0]. Eccentric orbits produce oscillatory instantaneous frequency evolution and recurring frequency passages (frequency can recur multiple times through coalescence), leading to periastron-localized rapid phase evolution or “bursts” near pericenter [d110908s0p0]. Tidal coupling in eccentric neutron-star binaries couples radial and angular motion and excites f-modes, producing extra orbital resonances (e.g., an orbital frequency ≃ one third of the f‑mode) that impart cumulative phase shifts up to ≈0.5 radians for e≈0.2 at 50 Hz and thus alter late‑inspiral phase evolution [d50408s0p0]. Pericenter f‑mode excitations transfer orbital energy into stellar oscillations, speeding orbital decay and advancing GW phase, with the phase shift growing with increasing eccentricity and depending on pericenter timing (orbital phase at observation) [d51623s0p0]. Sensitivity to and the observable imprint of eccentricity also depend on masses and mass ratio: detector sensitivity and waveform-model applicability vary across eccentricity, mass and mass-ratio space and are explicitly studied as functions of eccentricity, mass and mass ratio in catalog and model comparisons [d101479s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does nonzero eccentricity bias the inference of detector-frame masses and their conversion to source-frame masses and redshift — including systematic shifts in measured chirp mass and mass ratio, degeneracies between eccentricity and redshifted mass, and the impact on cosmological redshift estimates for typical LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA and LISA source distances?

How does the increased time- and frequency-domain complexity introduced by eccentric orbits (multiple harmonics, rapid phase evolution near periastron) affect Bayesian parameter estimation workflows — specifically posterior shapes (biases, multimodality), parameter degeneracies (eccentricity vs distance vs inclination), sampler convergence and computational cost, and resulting uncertainties on luminosity distance?

What concrete eccentric-binary waveform families and approximation schemes are available (e.g., PN-based eccentric inspiral waveforms, EOB models with eccentricity, inspiral-merger-ringdown hybrids, numerical-relativity eccentric catalogs, kludge/semianalytic LISA models), what are their stated validity ranges in eccentricity, mass ratio and spin, and what published estimates exist for their systematic errors or mismatches (e.g., mismatch vs eccentricity, bias in recovered parameters)?
sub_answers.text: Analytic 3PN Fourier-domain ready-to-use inspiral templates for moderately eccentric orbits (including amplitude corrections to 1PN and phase evolution to 3PN with eccentricity expansions and periastron-advance prescriptions) are available for compact binaries inspiraling along moderately eccentric orbits [d50914s0p0]. The non-spinning, inspiral-only EccentricFD approximant has been used for Bayesian parameter-estimation studies and sensitivity estimates, with stated sensitivity to eccentricities ≳0.05 at 10 Hz for current-generation detectors in GW‑like events [d44584s0p0]. Effective-one-body / waveform-model comparisons (e.g., TEOBResumS-Dali) and numerical-relativity catalogs (SXS and RIT) have been used together to evaluate detector sensitivity and waveform compatibility across eccentricity, mass and mass ratio [d101479s0p0]. Post-Newtonian adiabatic eccentric models have been directly compared to NR for e≈0.1 and shown phase agreement within ≈0.1 radians for ≈10 cycles and growing to ≈0.7 radians nearer merger, illustrating known phase-systematic trends of PN approximants versus NR for moderate eccentricity [d2843s0p0]. Waveform-validity ranges cited in studies include eccentricities up to e≤0.4 for early-warning and sky-localization analyses and applicability described as “moderately eccentric” for 3PN templates, while mismatch and phase-bias studies are reported via NR–PN phase differences and detector-sensitivity versus eccentricity curves in catalog/model comparisons [d110908s0p0][d2843s0p0][d101479s0p0].
